blocks.text: To the Arabs and the Chaldeans I add the ancient Hebrews, who plainly place צב tsab, or חרדון chardon, among the species of lizards. This will be made clear by two passages which I shall cite; many have already noticed them, but no one has yet explained them. The first is in the Talmudic tractate Cholin, ch. 9, fol. 127a, where the Hebrews hold that under the name צב tsab, forbidden in the Law, similar species are included, because after its kind was added. For the words of the Law run thus: These shall be unclean to you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth: the mole and the mouse, והצב למינהו, and the tsab after its [II, 476] kind. That is, they say: להביא העריד ובן־נפילים וסלמנדרא, to include the arod and the ben-nephilim and the salamander, as species close to the dhab. The more recent writers, indeed, do not know what ערוד arod and בן־נפילים ben-nephilim are here. But at least it is known that the salamander belongs to the lizard genus. Therefore צב tsab must be referred to the same genus. The matter will be plainer if we show what ערוד arod and בן־נפילים ben-nephilim are here. Elsewhere the former means the wild ass, the latter son of the giants, which seem to be beside the point. So the interpreters are at a loss here, and neither the Glossators of the Talmud nor the Lexicographers offer anything that looks like the truth. But the first word is corrupt, and instead of ערוד arod, or iruad, one should write עסוד isvvad. This is a white kind of lizard, living in the sands, to which the Arab poets compare the fingers of girls. Some call it عذفوط [ʿdhfwṭ] odphut and عضرفوط [ʿḍrfwṭ] adhraphut. Alcamus: العذفوط دويبة [col. 1055] بيضا ناعمة يشبة بها اصابع الجواري [al-ʿdhfwṭ duwaybba bayḍā nāʿima yshbh bihā aṣābiʿ al-jawārī], Alodphut, a small animal, white and pleasing, to which the fingers of girls are compared. And elsewhere: العضرفوط العذفوط او ذكر العظا [al-ʿḍrfwṭ al-ʿdhfwṭ aw dhakar al-ʿaẓā], Aladhraphut, the same as alodphut, or the male lizard. And again: العسود للعضرفوط من العظاء [al-ʿiswad lil-ʿḍrfwṭ min al-ʿaẓāʾ], Aliswad is said of the adraphut, of the lizard genus. Likewise: العسودة دويبة بضا يشبه بها بنان العذاري وتكني بنة النقا [al-ʿiswada duwaybba bḍā yushbih bihā banān al-ʿadhārī wa-tukannā bnt al-naqā], Aliswada, a small white animal, to which the fleshy tips of maidens' fingers are compared; it is surnamed Binth-onnakai, that is, daughter of the sand. Therefore, since ערוד is reckoned by the Talmudists among the species of lizards, by a slight change ערוד should be read as עסוד, so that the lizard we have described is meant. Unskilled scribes changed עסוד, which is little used and perhaps not known from elsewhere, into ערוד, which means something entirely different, namely the wild ass. It remains for us to say what animal the בן־נפילים ben-nephilim is, which is of the same kind as these. A man eminent in these studies, who today has no equal, rightly infers that this animal is aquatic, because we read in Shemot Rabbah, Sect. 15: ועיע את הימים והראהו את בן־הנפילים שנאמר קול יי על המים, He (God) moved the seas and showed him (Moses) Ben-nephilim, as it is said Ps. XXIX, 3: „The voice of the Lord is upon the waters. But the same man errs very seriously when, from the affinity of the words and the similarity of the animals (as he asserts), he infers that בן־נפילים ben-nephilim is the nauplius, or nautilus. For even if we grant that nephilim in some way echoes nauplius, there is still no similarity in the things themselves. For the nauplius, or nautilus, has nothing in common with the tsab, whether this word means a toad or a tortoise, as he would have it, or some species of lizard, which I hold most firmly. For lizards, toads and tortoises differ in their whole genus from the nauplius, or nautilus fish. Nor is it at all likely that the Hebrews derived their נפילים nephilim from the name nauplius, which is little used, [II, 477] and occurs nowhere, so far as I remember, except in a single passage of Pliny. Nor, again, was nauplius made from נפילים nephilim. For it is evident that this name was taken from the thing itself, and that the nautilus is called nauplius because it sails as if in a ship, from the noun ναῦς [naus] and the verb πλεῖν [plein]. What, then, is the בן־נפילים ben-nephilim? It certainly seems to be the Egyptian skink, of which Avicenna, book 2, in the chapter اسقنقور [isqanqūr] Iscancur, as the Arabs call the skink, says: هو ورل الماي يصاد من نيل مصر ويقولون انه من نسل التمساح اذا وضعه خارج الما ونشا خارجا [huwa waral al-māy yuṣād min nīl miṣr wa-yaqūlūn innahu min nasl al-timsāḥ idhā waḍaʿahu khārij al-mā wa-nashaʾa khārijan] It is the aquatic guaril, which is caught in Egypt on the bank of the Nile; they say it is born from the seed of the crocodile, when it sheds it out of the water, and that it grows up out of the water ^{(3)}. And again in the chapter سقنقور [saqanqūr] Scancur: ورل نيلي يصاد بمصر ويزعمون انه من نتاج التمساح في البر [waral nīlī yuṣād bi-miṣr wa-yazʿumūn annahu min nitāj al-timsāḥ fī al-barr] It is the Nilotic guaril, which they catch in Egypt, and [col. 1056] they say it is born on land from the seed of the crocodile. And Alkazuinius, after citing Avicenna: وقال غيره انه من نسل التمساح اذا وضعه خارج الما فما قصد الما صار تمساحا وما قصد البر صار سقنقورا [wa-qāla ghayruhu innahu min nasl al-timsāḥ idhā waḍaʿahu khārij al-mā fa-mā qaṣada al-mā ṣāra timsāḥan wa-mā qaṣada al-barr ṣāra saqanqūran] Others, he says, have said that it comes from the seed of the crocodile, when it casts it out of the water; and that whatever reaches the water becomes a crocodile, and whatever stays on land a skink. And Damir: الاسقنقور نوعان هندي ومصري فالمصري منه ما يتولد ببحر القلزم وهو يغتذي بالسمك في الما وفي البر بالقطا يسرطه كالحيات [al-isqanqūr nawʿān hindī wa-miṣrī fa-al-miṣrī minhu mā yatawallad bi-baḥr al-qulzum wa-huwa yaghtadhī bi-al-samak fī al-mā wa-fī al-barr bi-al-qaṭā yasruṭuhu ka-al-ḥayyāt] The skink is of two species, Indian and Egyptian. Among the Egyptian ones is one which is born in the sea of Kelzem (that is, the Red Sea), and feeds on fish in the water, and on land on pigeons, which it swallows like serpents. Since this is absurd, instead of بالقطا [bi-al-qaṭā], that is, on pigeons, one should read بالعظا [bi-al-ʿaẓā], on lizards. And further on, inquiring how the guaril and the skink differ from each other, he places the chief difference in this: أن ورل لا ياوي الا البراري الاسقنقور لا ياوي الا بالقرب من الما او فيه [anna waral lā yaʾwī illā al-barārī al-isqanqūr lā yaʾwī illā bi-al-qurb min al-mā aw fīhi] that the guaril lives only on land, but the skink only near [II, 478] the waters, or even in the waters themselves. And further on: لا نعرف اليوم في عصرنا الاسقنقور في ديار المصرية الا ببلاد الفيوم ومنها يجلب الي القاهرة لمن اعتني بطلبه ولا يصاد الا في ايام الشتا لانه اذا اشتد حليه البرد خرج الي البر فيصاد [lā naʿrif al-yawm fī ʿaṣrinā al-isqanqūr fī diyār al-miṣriyya illā bi-bilād al-fayyūm wa-minhā yujlab ilā al-qāhira li-man iʿtanā bi-ṭalabihi wa-lā yuṣād illā fī ayyām al-shitā li-annahu idhā ishtadda ḥlyh al-bard kharaja ilā al-barr fa-yuṣād] Today, in our age, we know of the skink nowhere in the Egyptian territory except in the province of Phium, from which it is brought to Cairo for whoever is concerned to seek it. It is caught only in winter; for, driven by the force of the cold, it comes out onto land and is caught there. And shortly after: يحل اكل الاسقنقور الهندي لانه سمك ويحتمل ان ياتي فيه وجه الحرمة لان له شبهين في البر احدهما احرام وهو الورل واخر حلال وهو الضب واما الاسقنقور المصري فهو حرام [col. 1057] لانه متولد من التمساح فهو حرام كاصله [yaḥillu akl al-isqanqūr al-hindī li-annahu samak wa-yuḥtamal an yaʾtī fīhi wajh al-ḥurma li-anna lahu shibhayn fī al-barr aḥaduhumā aḥrām wa-huwa al-waral wa-ākhar ḥalāl wa-huwa al-ḍabb wa-ammā al-isqanqūr al-miṣrī fa-huwa ḥarām li-annahu mutawallad min al-timsāḥ fa-huwa ḥarām ka-aṣlihi] It is lawful to eat the Indian skink, because it is a fish ^{(4)}, although an aspect of a forbidden thing may be ascribed to it, because on land the guaril and the dhab are similar to it, of which one is forbidden and the other permitted. But the Egyptian skink is forbidden, because it is born of the crocodile; therefore it is prohibited, like its root. Of the many things the Arabs say about the skink ^{(5)}, we have excerpted these few because they serve our purpose. From them three things follow. First, that the skink is contained under the same genus as the dhab and the guaril, since it resembles them in form. Second, that it is amphibious, and lives mostly in the waters of the Nile, and so also in the sea. Thus it can rightly be said that God moved את הימים, the seas, to show the skink to Moses. Although there is a fault in that word, and instead of הימים, that is the seas, one should read המים, the waters, with one small letter fewer, as what follows shows: As it is said, „The voice of the Lord is upon the waters“. Third, since the skink is believed (how truly, we do not now inquire) to be born from the seed of the crocodile, as the Arabs consistently write, it is clear why the Hebrews called it בן-נפילים, that is, son of the giants. For by the name giants the Orientals denote not only men but also any beasts of greater bulk. Thus an Arab writer in Damir: في جرادة خلق عشرة من جبابرة من الحيوان [fī jarāda khalq ʿashara min jabābira min al-ḥayawān] In the locust is the nature of ten giants among the animals; so it reads word for word, that is, of ten larger animals. Namely, as follows, the locust [II, 479] has the face of a horse, the eyes of an elephant, the neck of a bull, the horns of a stag, etc. On the same pattern the skink is called by the Hebrews son of the giants, that is, of the crocodiles, compared with which it is nothing but a very tiny animal. With these things thus explained, the truth will shine forth more and more if the whole passage is read, of which we have cited only a part. It runs thus: God stirred the waters to show him (Moses) the son of the giants, as it is said Psalm. XXIX, 3: „The voice of the Lord is upon the waters“. He stirred the earth to show him the צב tsab, as it is written Psalm. XXIX, 8: „The voice of the Lord makes the desert give birth“. He stirred fire to show him the salamander, as it is said Psal. XXIX, 7: „The voice of the Lord hews out flames of fire“. Thus from three elements are drawn three animals of different species but of the same genus: the son of the giants, or of the crocodiles, the skink, from the waters, in which it mostly lives; the צב tsab from the earth, to which it is so attached, as if to the soil, that it never goes down to the waters, as we proved above ^{d)}; and finally the salamander from fire, in which many wrongly suppose it is born and on which it feeds.
